title: Read Replicas
subtitle: Scaling read-heavy workloads while solving replication lag anomalies: Read-Your-Writes, Monotonic Reads, and LSN pinning.
keyTakeaways: Read replicas scale read-heavy applications (10:1 to 100:1 read-to-write ratios) by offloading queries from the primary database instance.
Asynchronous replication lag causes read-after-write anomalies: a user updates their profile, refreshes the page, and observes their old data.
Mitigate replication lag anomalies using Read-Your-Own-Writes routing: pin user reads to the primary database for 5-10 seconds following a write.

sections.heading: Consistency Anomalies Caused by Replication Lag
sections.body: Deploying read replicas is the standard pattern for scaling relational databases. However, because replication between primary and replicas is almost always asynchronous to keep write latency low, replicas lag behind the primary by milliseconds to seconds under load. This lag introduces severe client anomalies.
bullets: Read-Your-Writes Anomaly: A user changes their email address and clicks Save. The write commits to the primary. The browser immediately requests the updated profile, which routes to a read replica lagging by 500ms. The user sees their old email and assumes the save failed.

Monotonic Read Inversion: A user refreshes a comment thread twice. The first read hits a caught-up replica and shows 10 comments. The second read hits a lagging replica and shows 8 comments. The user observes time travel.
Replica Lag Spikes: Long-running analytical queries, batch migrations, or network saturation on replicas can inflate lag from 10ms to tens of seconds.

sections.heading: Architectural Patterns for Replica Routing
sections.body: Application architectures employ three common patterns to route traffic across primary and replica pools cleanly.
bullets: Connection-Level Splitting: Application code or ORMs maintain two distinct connection pools: `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` routes to replicas, while standard transactions route to primary.
Database Proxy Routing: Reverse proxies like ProxySQL or AWS RDS Proxy inspect incoming SQL statements; queries starting with `SELECT` route to replicas, while `INSERT/UPDATE` route to the primary.

LSN Watermarking: The primary returns its Log Sequence Number (LSN) upon commit. The client passes this token on subsequent reads; replicas serve the request only if their local replay LSN matches or exceeds the client's token.

tradeOffs.pros: Completely eliminates user confusion after mutations; simple to implement via Redis session keys.
tradeOffs.cons: Momentarily routes read traffic for active users to the primary, increasing primary load.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Interactive consumer web apps, social profile updates, and settings dashboards.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees mathematically exact consistency without over-routing traffic to the primary.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires database engine support for Global Transaction IDs (GTID) and client token propagation.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Financial accounting portals, order status tracking, and enterprise SaaS.

interviewTip: Whenever proposing read replicas in a design interview, anticipate the interviewer's next question: 'Because replication is asynchronous, we must prevent read-your-writes anomalies. We will store a timestamp in Redis whenever a user updates data and route that specific user's reads to the primary for the next 5 seconds, ensuring they immediately see their changes.'
